attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, in his own voice. He is not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: This is a firm, categorical present-tense claim that profits and returns 'aren't happening at all'. In context, 'they' means the AI industry and the hyperscaler leaders. The normalised wording leaves out the 'tangible proof' phrase, but the contract treats that phrase as reinforcing the financial claim, which is reasonable.

contract.note: The categorical plain reading is an ordinary one. The evaluator chose the target quarter and the profit measure. The contract also requires a matching accounting basis before it will score the claim, which effectively blocks a score. The result depends on these evaluator choices.

evidence.note: KPMG survey with fieldwork in the target quarter: 8% of firms self-report established ROI. These are self-reported estimates, not AI-specific net profits or returns with costs counted. Under the contract they cannot refute the claim.

The same KPMG survey: 64% report meaningful business value, a category that includes operational benefits. This weighs against 'not at all' but is not a measured financial return, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence is self-reported survey data on business value and ROI. Neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition is met. The survey results cut against the absolute wording, but they do not document AI-specific profits or net returns on a matching basis. The outcome stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: This is a causal claim that AI data-center demand depends on subsidies. The normalised wording says 'venture subsidies' only, but the context also points to hyperscaler support. The contract includes both, which is closer to the source.

contract.note: Narrowing the claim to commercial AI demand fits the context. The scope of 'data centers' and of 'these subsidies', and the evaluator-chosen quarter, all shape the result. The counterfactual of what demand would remain without subsidies is hard to measure.

evidence.note: JLL estimate of AI's share of 2025 workloads. It covers an earlier period and says nothing about whether customers are funded by subsidies.
CSC company blog on building the LUMI-AI public research data center. This is outside the commercial demand the claim discusses, and it does not settle the claim.

reviews.rationale: No evidence traces commercial AI data-center payments to how customers are funded, or shows how much demand would remain without subsidies. Both items are context only, so the causal claim cannot be settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps both linked parts: the named startups survive only on VC money, so a large share of each provider's API revenue depends on those subsidies.

contract.note: Fair. It does not invent a threshold for 'large chunk', it treats the providers separately, and it separates having VC funding from depending on it to survive. The quarter is the evaluator's choice.

evidence.note: Lovable's December 2025 Series B announcement, a company disclosure from before the target quarter. It shows VC funding, not that Lovable needs it to survive.
Anthropic company disclosure that it has large enterprise customers. It does not give API revenue shares by customer funding, so it neither supports nor refutes the claim.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no cash-flow or survival-dependence records for Perplexity or Lovable. It has no breakdown of either provider's API revenue by customer funding source. Both items are context only, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own prediction in his newsletter.

semantics.note: 'I believe we are on course for a truly horrible crash' is a firm expectation, so it is scored as a forecast. The consequences framed with 'may' are hedged and are rightly left out. No deadline is given.

contract.note: The contract's reading of a broad, severe AI-sector collapse is the ordinary one. It does not invent a deadline or a size threshold, and it does not treat continued growth as a contradiction. Deciding what counts as a 'crash' is left to the evaluator.

evidence.note: Sherlund data on the October 9–23 selloff: hyperscalers fell 5.9% and datacenter enablers 18.2%, with earnings estimates steady. This shows stress but not the broad collapse the contract requires.
PitchBook-NVCA: record VC investment through Q3 2026, mostly in AI. There is no financing collapse yet, but this cannot disprove a future crash.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. The October selloff is significant but uneven and falls short of the broad, severe collapse the early-resolution rule requires. Record AI venture funding through Q3 shows no financing collapse. With no conclusive event and no deadline, the forecast cannot yet be scored.
